title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
authors: James A. Kulik, J. D. Fletcher
abstract: This review describes a meta-analysis of findings from 50 controlled evaluations of intelligent computer tutoring systems. The median effect of intelligent tutoring in the 50 evaluations was to raise test scores 0.66 standard deviations over conventional levels, or from the 50th to the 75th percentile. However, the amount of improvement found in an evaluation depended to a great extent on whether improvement was measured on locally developed or standardized tests, suggesting that alignment of test and instructional objectives is a critical determinant of evaluation results. The review also describes findings from two groups of evaluations that did not meet all of the selection requirements for the meta-analysis: six evaluations with nonconventional control groups and four with flawed implementations of intelligent tutoring systems. Intelligent tutoring effects in these evaluations were small, suggesting that evaluation results are also affected by the nature of control treatments and the adequacy of program implementations.
explain_beginner: This paper looked at 50 studies of computer tutoring systems, which are programs that teach students and adjust to their needs. On average, students using these systems scored better than those in regular classes, moving from the middle of the pack to the top quarter. But the size of the improvement depended on the test used. Gains were bigger on tests made by the local school than on standard nationwide tests. The authors also note that poorly run programs or weak comparison groups led to smaller gains. So how well a system is used and how it is measured both matter.
explain_business: This analysis of 50 controlled studies shows intelligent tutoring can raise test scores substantially, with a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations, roughly moving an average student to the 75th percentile. However, results depend heavily on how success is measured. Gains were much larger on locally made tests than on standardized ones, and weak implementations or unsuitable comparison groups produced little benefit. For decision makers, this means pilot results can look better than real world impact if tests are not independent. Invest in proper implementation and use standardized measures to judge whether a tutoring system truly works before scaling it.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations of intelligent tutoring systems. The median effect was 0.66 standard deviations over conventional instruction, equivalent to a shift from the 50th to the 75th percentile. Effect size varied strongly with the outcome measure: locally developed tests showed larger gains than standardized tests, indicating that alignment between test content and instructional objectives shapes results. Two additional groups failing selection criteria were examined: six evaluations with nonconventional control groups and four with flawed implementations. Both showed small effects, suggesting control treatment design and implementation fidelity also influence reported effectiveness.
